analysis.one_liner: Bars federal judges, including Supreme Court justices, from accepting most gifts from people with business before the courts.
analysis.headline: A bill to ban most gifts to federal judges died in committee without a vote at the end of the 118th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would write a binding gift rule into federal law for every federal judge, including the nine Supreme Court justices. Judges generally could not accept anything worth $50 or more from a single source, or more than $100 a year from one source, and gifts to their relatives would count against them. The Justice Department could sue violators for civil penalties up to $50,000, and knowing violations could bring criminal penalties. The bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing or vote before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people who appear before federal courts. Judges decide cases brought by corporations, wealthy individuals, and political interests; a judge who accepts paid trips or luxury hospitality from people with likely business before the court risks the appearance — and reality — of a tilted playing field. The bill would make such gifts illegal for all federal judges, including Supreme Court justices, with real penalties, so litigants and the public could trust that rulings are not repaid in vacations and lodging.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Everyone who appears before federal courts

how_it_helps.text: Sets a hard cap: judges generally cannot accept any gift worth $50 or more from a single source, or more than $100 total from one source in a year, with items of fair-market value paid for, gifts from relatives, and a narrow list of exceptions carved out.

Adds teeth that current Supreme Court ethics rules lack: the Judicial Conference must refer suspected violations to the Attorney General, who can seek civil penalties up to $50,000; knowing violations can bring fines and up to a year in prison.

Gifts to a judge's relative count as gifts to the judge when given because of the judge's position, closing the family-membership workaround; the Supreme Court and Judicial Conference must issue implementing rules within 180 days.

analysis.who_pays: Federal judges and Supreme Court justices, who would lose the ability to accept gifts, paid travel, and luxury hospitality from anyone with interests likely to come before their court. Industries and wealthy litigants with active or likely court business could no longer legally court judges with trips and entertainment.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal judges and well-funded court litigants

drawbacks.text: The bill still allows personal hospitality from non-litigant individuals — use of a private residence or resort owned by a friend — up to the annual IRS gift-tax exclusion (roughly $18,000 in 2024), so lavish vacations hosted by wealthy friends would remain largely legal even when the friend's interests rarely, but do, come before the court.

Enforcement depends heavily on the Judicial Conference and on waivers that a Supreme Court justice may request from the Chief Justice for expensive seminar travel, meaning the judiciary largely polices itself; the criminal provision also requires proving a knowing and willful violation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits — enforceable gift limits with real penalties for all federal judges, including the Supreme Court — come at almost no public cost. The bill is narrow by design: it leaves personal hospitality from non-party individuals up to a generous annual exclusion (the IRS gift exclusion), which is a real but limited loophole. Weighed against the documented stakes of litigants and industries with matters before the courts, the trade is strongly favorable to the public.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never acted on it, and Congress adjourned, killing the bill.

narrative.text: Introduced September 25, 2024, the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee — its only action.
The bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote, and it died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
It attracted five cosponsors, all Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the committee's agenda was controlled by the majority.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Judges who receive gifts and subsidized travel from litigants and interest groups keep that benefit; the court system avoids the cost of new enforcement machinery. Anyone harmed by a judge's conflicts remains without a federal statutory remedy.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Judges and gift-giving litigants; public got nothing

for.name: Sen. Ben Ray Luján
for.what_they_did: Introduced the High Court Gift Ban Act in the Senate.

for.name: Sens. Peter Welch, Chris Van Hollen, and Ron Wyden
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors when the bill was introduced.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee (118th Congress)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill after it was referred.

against.name: Senate Republicans (49)
against.what_they_did: None of the 49 Republican senators cosponsored the bill, leaving it without any bipartisan cosponsor in a chamber where the party controlled the agenda.

sides.party_line_note: All five cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican cosponsored, and the bill never advanced in the Republican-run Senate.

industries.industry: Litigants, law firms, and corporate interests with cases before the courts
industries.note: These are the 'prohibited sources' the bill targets: parties and interest groups whose matters come before judges could no longer legally fund their travel, lodging, and entertainment. The ban applies to sitting federal judges.

industries.industry: Sitting federal judges, including Supreme Court justices
industries.note: Judges would lose access to gifts and subsidized travel above small thresholds and face civil and criminal penalties for violations, with the judiciary required to write compliance rules within 180 days.
